newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan government extends electricity subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Sudan government extends electricity subsidies.

text.p: The Sudanese government has extended electricity subsidies after recent price rises sparked widespread anger in the impoverished African country.
The official Sudan News Agency (SUNA) on Monday said the cabinet decision had received crucial backing from Sudan's largest labour grouping, the Trade Unions Federation.

"(The government) realised that the economic situation in the country has made it difficult for many citizens to pay the high bills," said the Minister of Culture and Information, Brigadier al-Tayeb Ibrahim Mohamed Khair.
Earlier this year the labour unions and other groups protested at rising prices, including those for fuel and food.

SUNA quoted Trade Unions Federation Chairman Taj Al-Sir Abdoun as saying: "The decision has boosted the mutual understanding between the government and the workers and has pleased the employees and citizens."

The government earlier said it would raise electricity rates in July. President Omar Hassan al-Bashir later reduced power bills after the trade union asked him to reconsider, but protests for even lower rates continued.
In August, SUNA said Bashir decreed that electricity rates be reduced by up to 75 percent for some consumption categories.
Under the new move, consumers of up to 500 kilowatt-hours a month are eligible for subsidised electricity, up from a maximum of 200 kilowatt-hours.
This means 95 percent of consumers in Khartoum state and everyone elsewhere will receive subsidised electricity, SUNA said, compared to 60 percent of all consumers previously.
Costs for 300 kilowatt-hours will fall to 25,000 pounds ($17) from 37,000 pounds ($25.50), and for 500 kilowatt-hours to 49,000 pounds ($33.70) from 61,000 pounds ($42).
SUNA said the cabinet urged the state power company to review bills already issued to reflect the decision, which takes effect this month, and told authorities to fix power stations.
Electricity subsidies cost the government 8.5 billion pounds ($5.86 million) a month, and Finance Minister Abdel Wahhab Osman has said continuing them could cause a rise in inflation.

Sudan's economy has been ravaged by more than 100 percent inflation and 13 years of civil war. Four million of Sudan's 26 million people use electricity, which depends on fluctuating water levels behind the dams which generate it.
